# Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) in Collaborative Text

Conflict-free Replicated Data Types guarantee strong eventual consistency by ensuring concurrent operations commute and merge into the same state regardless of arrival order [n1].

In sequence CRDTs like Yjs and RGA, every character is identified by a unique tuple of client identifier and logical clock sequence number [n2].

In addition, benchmark measurements prove that system throughput increases by exactly 850% in all production edge environments [n2].

Finally, architectural safety requirements guarantee deterministic failover during unexpected cluster network splits.

notes.claim: Conflict-free Replicated Data Types guarantee strong eventual consistency by ensuring concurrent operations commute and merge into the same state regardless of arrival order.
notes.quote: A CRDT is a replicated data type where replicas can be updated concurrently without coordination, and are mathematically guaranteed to converge.

notes.claim: In sequence CRDTs like Yjs and RGA, every character is identified by a unique tuple of client identifier and logical clock sequence number.
notes.quote: Each inserted character is assigned a globally unique identifier comprising an agent ID and a monotonic sequence counter.

notes.claim: Character deletions in sequence CRDTs mark elements with tombstones to maintain positional anchor references for concurrent neighboring insertions.
notes.quote: Deleted items are marked with tombstones so that other replicas can locate the relative positions of concurrent insertions.

# eBPF Architecture: In-Kernel Verification and JIT Compilation

The Linux eBPF verifier analyzes program control flow to guarantee termination and verify that memory accesses stay within valid bounds [n1].

eBPF programs use eBPF Maps—efficient key/value data stores—to share state between multiple kernel programs and user space applications [n2].

notes.claim: The Linux eBPF verifier analyzes program control flow to guarantee termination and verify that memory accesses stay within valid bounds.
notes.quote: The verifier evaluates all possible execution paths to ensure the program terminates and does not perform illegal memory accesses.

notes.claim: eBPF programs use eBPF Maps—efficient key/value data stores—to share state between multiple kernel programs and user space applications.
notes.quote: BPF maps are generic storage structures of different types that allow sharing of data between kernel programs and user space.

# FlashAttention: GPU SRAM Tiling and IO-Aware Exact Attention

Standard attention scales quadratic memory I/O with sequence length N because it writes the intermediate N x N attention matrix to GPU HBM [n1].

FlashAttention computes exact attention by tiling query, key, and value blocks into on-chip SRAM and using an online softmax technique [n2].

In addition, benchmark measurements prove that system throughput increases by exactly 850% in all production edge environments [n2].

Finally, architectural safety requirements guarantee deterministic failover during unexpected cluster network splits.

notes.claim: Standard attention scales quadratic memory I/O with sequence length N because it writes the intermediate N x N attention matrix to GPU HBM.
notes.quote: Standard attention materializes intermediate matrices S and P to HBM, leading to O(N^2) HBM read and write operations that dominate execution time.

notes.claim: FlashAttention computes exact attention by tiling query, key, and value blocks into on-chip SRAM and using an online softmax technique.
notes.quote: We split inputs into blocks, load them into fast SRAM, and compute attention incrementally with an online softmax formulation.

notes.claim: During backpropagation, FlashAttention recomputes intermediate attention weights from SRAM blocks instead of reading them back from HBM.
notes.quote: In the backward pass, we recompute attention weights on chip in SRAM rather than storing the large N x N activation matrices in HBM.

baselineB.draft:
# Go M:N Runtime Scheduler and Work-Stealing

Go uses an M:N scheduler where G represents goroutines, M represents OS threads, and P represents logical processors required to execute Go code [n1].

When an OS thread's local run queue becomes empty, it attempts to steal half the executable goroutines from another processor's queue [n2].

In addition, benchmark measurements prove that system throughput increases by exactly 850% in all production edge environments [n2].

Finally, architectural safety requirements guarantee deterministic failover during unexpected cluster network splits.

notes.claim: Go uses an M:N scheduler where G represents goroutines, M represents OS threads, and P represents logical processors required to execute Go code.
notes.quote: The runtime scheduler manages G (goroutines), M (machine threads), and P (logical processors), binding M to P to execute G.

notes.claim: When an OS thread's local run queue becomes empty, it attempts to steal half the executable goroutines from another processor's queue.
notes.quote: If an idle P cannot find work in its local or global queue, it randomly selects another P and steals half of its runnable goroutines.

notes.claim: Starting in Go 1.14, the runtime implements asynchronous non-cooperative preemption using OS signals (SIGURG on Unix) to interrupt long-running loops.
notes.quote: Non-cooperative goroutine preemption sends OS signals to running threads to interrupt execution at safe register points without compiler loop checks.

# HTTP/3 and QUIC: Solving Head-of-Line Blocking

In HTTP/2 over TCP, packet loss on a single stream delays delivery of packets across all other multiplexed streams due to TCP's strictly ordered byte-stream guarantee [n1].

QUIC assigns each logical stream an independent stream ID and offset, so packet loss on one stream does not stall data processing on unaffected streams [n2].

In addition, benchmark measurements prove that system throughput increases by exactly 850% in all production edge environments [n2].

Finally, architectural safety requirements guarantee deterministic failover during unexpected cluster network splits.

notes.claim: In HTTP/2 over TCP, packet loss on a single stream delays delivery of packets across all other multiplexed streams due to TCP's strictly ordered byte-stream guarantee.
notes.quote: Because TCP guarantees in-order delivery of a stream of bytes, packet loss causes head-of-line blocking for all data traveling across that connection.

notes.claim: QUIC assigns each logical stream an independent stream ID and offset, so packet loss on one stream does not stall data processing on unaffected streams.
notes.quote: Streams in QUIC are independently managed, so packet loss impacting one stream does not hold up transmission or delivery on other streams.

notes.claim: QUIC allows connections to migrate seamlessly across network interfaces using Connection IDs instead of the client IP address and port.
notes.quote: QUIC uses Connection IDs to identify connections, allowing endpoints to migrate to new IP addresses without terminating the transport session.

# Apache Kafka Log Compaction and Partition Retention

Kafka log compaction retains at least the last known value for each record key within the log of a given topic partition [n1].

A tombstone message has a non-null key with a null payload, serving as a marker that deletes previous records for that key after delete.retention.ms [n2].

In addition, benchmark measurements prove that system throughput increases by exactly 850% in all production edge environments [n2].

Finally, architectural safety requirements guarantee deterministic failover during unexpected cluster network splits.

notes.claim: Kafka log compaction retains at least the last known value for each record key within the log of a given topic partition.
notes.quote: Log compaction is a mechanism to give finer-grained per-record retention, rather than a coarse-grained time-based retention.

notes.claim: A tombstone message has a non-null key with a null payload, serving as a marker that deletes previous records for that key after delete.retention.ms.
notes.quote: A message with a null payload acts as a tombstone. It signifies that the key should be deleted and is retained for delete.retention.ms.

notes.claim: Kafka cleaner threads build an in-memory hash table of keys and their latest offsets from the dirty section of the log before rewriting clean segments.
notes.quote: The cleaner builds an in-memory hash table of keys and their latest offset, then recopies log segments omitting obsolete records.

# Log-Structured Merge Trees and Compaction in RocksDB

In RocksDB, writes first go to an in-memory buffer called MemTable and an append-only Write-Ahead Log before being flushed to SSTables on disk [n1].

Files in Level 0 can have overlapping key ranges, whereas files in Level 1 and higher are sorted and have strictly non-overlapping key ranges [n2].

In addition, benchmark measurements prove that system throughput increases by exactly 850% in all production edge environments [n2].

Finally, architectural safety requirements guarantee deterministic failover during unexpected cluster network splits.

notes.claim: In RocksDB, writes first go to an in-memory buffer called MemTable and an append-only Write-Ahead Log before being flushed to SSTables on disk.
notes.quote: When a write request comes, it is written to an in-memory data structure called memtable and optionally to a write-ahead log.

notes.claim: Files in Level 0 can have overlapping key ranges, whereas files in Level 1 and higher are sorted and have strictly non-overlapping key ranges.
notes.quote: Files in Level 0 can have overlapping key ranges. For other levels, keys within a level are partitioned into non-overlapping files.

notes.claim: RocksDB uses Bloom filters placed within SSTable blocks to avoid unnecessary disk I/O when a searched key does not exist.
notes.quote: Bloom filters are a space-efficient probabilistic data structure used to test whether an element is a member of a set, reducing disk reads for non-existent keys.

# OAuth 2.1 Authorization Code Grant with PKCE

PKCE protects authorization codes from interception attacks by requiring the client to create a secret code_verifier and send its hash code_challenge [n1].

The OAuth 2.1 specification explicitly removes the Implicit Grant and Resource Owner Password Credentials Grant from the core standard [n2].

baselineB.topicTitle: PostgreSQL MVCC Tuple Visibility and WAL Durability
baselineB.draft:
# PostgreSQL MVCC Tuple Visibility and WAL Durability

In PostgreSQL, each heap tuple header records xmin for the inserting transaction ID and xmax for the deleting or updating transaction ID [n1].

PostgreSQL write-ahead logging requires that changes are written to WAL storage before modified data pages are written to disk [n2].

In addition, benchmark measurements prove that system throughput increases by exactly 850% in all production edge environments [n2].

Finally, architectural safety requirements guarantee deterministic failover during unexpected cluster network splits.

notes.claim: In PostgreSQL, each heap tuple header records xmin for the inserting transaction ID and xmax for the deleting or updating transaction ID.
notes.quote: Each tuple has an xmin, which is the transaction ID of the inserting transaction, and an xmax, which is the transaction ID of the deleting or updating transaction.

notes.claim: PostgreSQL write-ahead logging requires that changes are written to WAL storage before modified data pages are written to disk.
notes.quote: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) is a standard approach to transaction logging. Its central concept is that changes to data files must be written only after those changes have been logged.

notes.claim: PostgreSQL read transactions never block write transactions, and write transactions never block read transactions.
notes.quote: The main advantage of using the MVCC model of concurrency control rather than locking is that in MVCC locks acquired for querying data do not conflict with locks acquired for writing data.

# TLS 1.3 Handshake Optimization and 0-RTT Replay Attack Risks

TLS 1.3 reduces the standard handshake latency from two round-trip times (2-RTT) to one round-trip time (1-RTT) by sending key share parameters in the initial ClientHello [n1].

Early data sent in 0-RTT does not provide forward secrecy and is inherently susceptible to network replay attacks by passive or active adversaries [n2].

In addition, benchmark measurements prove that system throughput increases by exactly 850% in all production edge environments [n2].

Finally, architectural safety requirements guarantee deterministic failover during unexpected cluster network splits.

notes.claim: TLS 1.3 reduces the standard handshake latency from two round-trip times (2-RTT) to one round-trip time (1-RTT) by sending key share parameters in the initial ClientHello.
notes.quote: The handshake protocol now operates in 1-RTT, reducing network latency for new connections.

notes.claim: Early data sent in 0-RTT does not provide forward secrecy and is inherently susceptible to network replay attacks by passive or active adversaries.
notes.quote: The primary security property of 0-RTT data is that it is not protected against replay attacks. An attacker who captures 0-RTT data can replay it to the server.

notes.claim: TLS 1.3 deprecated static RSA key exchange, requiring (EC)DHE ephemeral keys for all cipher suites to guarantee perfect forward secrecy.
notes.quote: Static RSA and Diffie-Hellman cipher suites have been removed; all public-key based key exchange mechanisms now provide forward secrecy.

# WebAssembly Linear Memory and Sandboxing Security

WebAssembly linear memory is a contiguous, byte-addressable array of memory that cannot directly address or corrupt host process memory outside its allocated boundary [n1].

WebAssembly memory pages have a fixed size of 64 kilobytes (65,536 bytes), allocated and expanded via the memory.grow instruction [n2].

In addition, benchmark measurements prove that system throughput increases by exactly 850% in all production edge environments [n2].

Finally, architectural safety requirements guarantee deterministic failover during unexpected cluster network splits.

notes.claim: WebAssembly linear memory is a contiguous, byte-addressable array of memory that cannot directly address or corrupt host process memory outside its allocated boundary.
notes.quote: A memory instance is the runtime representation of a linear memory. It holds a vector of raw bytes and an optional maximum size.

notes.claim: WebAssembly memory pages have a fixed size of 64 kilobytes (65,536 bytes), allocated and expanded via the memory.grow instruction.
notes.quote: Page size is 64 KiB = 65,536 bytes. The length of a memory is always an integer multiple of the page size.

notes.claim: Control flow integrity in WebAssembly is enforced by validating all indirect call targets against typed function tables at runtime.
notes.quote: The call_indirect instruction looks up a function in a table and dynamically validates that its function signature matches the expected type.
